content: Individuals with chronic plaque psoriasis frequently experience lesions on the scalp. The presence of hair complicates the application of treatments, and the adjacent facial skin is particularly sensitive to topical therapies. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of topical treatments specifically for scalp psoriasis. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Skin Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and LILACS, up to August 2015. Additional sources included five trial registries, abstracts from six psoriasis-specific conferences, and reference lists of included studies. The focus was on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving participants of all ages with scalp psoriasis, using parallel-group, cross-over, or within-patient designs. Two independent authors selected studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Discrepancies were resolved by consulting a third author. The primary outcomes evaluated were clearance or response as assessed by the Investigator Global Assessment (IGA), quality of life improvements, adverse events leading to treatment withdrawal, and response as assessed by the Patient Global Assessment (PGA). Results were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences (MD) with 95% CI for continuous outcomes. Meta-analyses were performed using a random-effects model when data were sufficiently homogeneous. The number needed to treat to benefit (NNTB) was also calculated. Topical corticosteroids were categorized by potency (mild, moderate, high, very high) based on the German classification system. A total of 59 RCTs involving 11,561 participants were included. Thirty of these studies were conducted or sponsored by the manufacturers of the study medications. The risk of bias varied significantly across studies, with many failing to report randomization methods or allocation concealment. Most studies were short-term (less than six months), with only one trial extending to 12 months. The analysis focused on three major comparisons: corticosteroids versus vitamin D, a two-compound combination of corticosteroids and vitamin D versus corticosteroid monotherapy, and the two-compound combination versus vitamin D monotherapy. For clearance as assessed by the IGA, corticosteroids were more effective than vitamin D (RR 1.82; 95% CI 1.52 to 2.18; NNTB = 8; moderate-quality evidence). The two-compound combination was statistically superior to corticosteroid monotherapy, but the additional benefit was small (RR 1.22; 95% CI 1.08 to 1.36; NNTB = 17; moderate-quality evidence). The two-compound combination was more effective than vitamin D alone (RR 2.28; 95% CI 1.87 to 2.78; NNTB = 6; high-quality evidence). For treatment response as assessed by the IGA, corticosteroids were again more effective than vitamin D (RR 2.09; 95% CI 1.80 to 2.41; NNTB = 4; high-quality evidence). The two-compound combination was better than corticosteroid monotherapy, but the additional benefit was minimal (RR 1.15; 95% CI 1.06 to 1.25; NNTB = 13; moderate-quality evidence). The two-compound combination was also more effective than vitamin D alone (RR 2.31; 95% CI 1.75 to 3.04; NNTB = 3; moderate-quality evidence). Quality of life data were poorly reported and insufficient for meta-analysis. Corticosteroids caused fewer withdrawals due to adverse events compared to vitamin D (RR 0.22; 95% CI 0.11 to 0.42; moderate-quality evidence). The two-compound combination and corticosteroid monotherapy showed no significant difference in adverse event-related withdrawals (RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.42 to 1.88; moderate-quality evidence). However, the two-compound combination led to fewer withdrawals due to adverse events compared to vitamin D (RR 0.19; 95% CI 0.11 to 0.36; high-quality evidence). None of the studies specified the types of adverse events leading to withdrawal. For treatment response as assessed by the PGA, corticosteroids were more effective than vitamin D (RR 1.48; 95% CI 1.28 to 1.72; NNTB = 5; moderate-quality evidence). The two-compound combination was statistically better than corticosteroid monotherapy, but the clinical benefit was negligible (RR 1.13; 95% CI 1.06 to 1.20; NNTB = 13; high-quality evidence). The two-compound combination was more effective than vitamin D (RR 1.76; 95% CI 1.46 to 2.12; NNTB = 4; moderate-quality evidence). Common adverse events across all three interventions included local irritation, skin pain, and folliculitis. Systemic adverse events were rare and likely unrelated to the treatments. The two-compound combination, corticosteroids, and vitamin D monotherapy were all more effective than placebo. Corticosteroids of moderate, high, and very high potency demonstrated similar efficacy and tolerability. However, the review had limitations in evaluating other topical treatments such as salicylic acid, tar, and dithranol. In conclusion, the two-compound combination and corticosteroid monotherapy were more effective and safer than vitamin D monotherapy. Given the comparable safety profile and the marginal additional benefit of the two-compound combination, monotherapy with generic topical corticosteroids may be an acceptable option for short-term treatment. Future RCTs should focus on the impact of specific therapies on quality of life and include long-term assessments (6 to 12 months).
